By Gordon Cramb
Amsterdam

Dutch Cannabis Vote Irks Cabinet

The Dutch parliament yesterday voted to decriminalise the wholesale trade in cannabis, in a surprise outcome that has wrong-footed the cabinet. A narrow majority backed a motion aimed at removing the anomaly under which licensed " coffee shops " are allowed to hold and sell small quantities of the drug, while their suppliers remain open to prosecution.

Policy; Published In The Most Improbable Place

The move is likely to draw renewed international scrutiny of the Netherlands' liberal drugs policy. Benk Korthals, justice minister, said: " This sends the wrong signal, and iscontrary to international treaties. "
(MarijuanaNews note: Korthals is a member of the Conservative Liberal Party – that is really its name – which is a part of the coalition government dominated by the Social Democrats, the party of Prime Minister Wim Kok. The " wrong signal " cliché aside, his primary concern is avoiding flack from the other EU countries, notably France. Switzerland is not a member of the EU, nor is it a signatory to the various prohibitionist treaties, so it is free to do as it wants.)
See
Swiss Upper House Approves Proposal to Legalize Marijuana Use

The centre-left cabinet is to discuss the issue on Friday, at its last meeting before the summer recess. But he indicated that he would not draw up legislation to comply with the vote.

As many as 60 Dutch local authorities, which regulate the coffee shops, are in favour of the change. Edumond d'Hondt, mayor of the eastern city of Nijmegen, said he would fight any resistance by the cabinet, threatening a lawsuit if it did not comply with the wish of parliament.
(MarijuanaNews note: In Holland, the policy towards coffee shops has been decentralized so that the municipalities make the decisions. Earlier this year, approximately 20 of the largest cities, other than the largest five, Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Utrecht, etc., petitioned the government to do this, and the frantic Justice Minister quickly rejected the notion. The five largest cities have quietly adopted an informal policy along these lines.

At this point, most of the cities and towns of any size have now backed de facto legalization of cultivation. This vote in the parliament demonstrates that there is now a majority in the Parliament for " legalization " -- although they won’t call it that, in deference to their prohibitionist neighbors.)


The best hope of ministers appeared last night to be the holding of a fresh parliamentary debate later in the year, at which the 73-72 vote could be reversed.
(MarijuanaNews note: There are 150 members of Parliament.)

After a review of policy on " soft " drugs, Mr Korthals said in April that enforcement efforts would be aimed mainly at illegal cultivation within the country as well as imports.

Greenhouse cultivation has been on the rise, although the International Narcotics Control Board, a United Nations agency, in February said the country's initiatives in curbing the growing of the drug were exemplary.
(MarijuanaNews note: The treaties do not have any enforcement mechanism, and if the UN narks say that the Dutch are actually violating the treaties, they run the risk of voiding them.)

Unlicensed points of sale, such as private houses and delivery services, were spreading rapidly in cities, according to the justice ministry. That came amid a fall in the number of coffee shops, to a national total of 840 from 1,200 five years ago.
